pdf_text.text: NIGERIA JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAMAWA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.intdtm.iom.int/nigeria For further information, please contact DTM Nigeria DATE OF DATA COLLECTION: 2 and 3 AUGUST 2025 DATE OF PUBLICATION: 19 AUGUST 2025 OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and September. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. On 2 and 3 August 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in close coordination and collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) Zonal Office, the Adamawa State Emergency Management Agency (ADSEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the International Rescue Committee (IRC), the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), the World Health Organization (WHO) and 20 other humanitarian partners in Yola South LGA, conducted a Joint Rapid Assessment (JRA) in response to a flash flood incident that occurred overnight across seven communities located across four wards of Bako, Bole Yolde Pate, Makama A and Makama B of Yola South local government area (LGA), Adamawa State. The assessment aimed to understand the extent of the flood’s impact on the affected population and infrastructure and to inform government and humanitarian partners on urgent needs, vulnerabilities, and displacement dynamics. The joint assessment identified a total of 15,128 individuals (or 3,057 households) who were affected by the flood. Of these, 4,890 individuals (or 720 households) were displaced within the host- community, while 7,148 individuals (1,853 households) remained in their community despite being significantly impacted. Shelter damage was widespread: 16 per cent of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 38 per cent were partially damaged, and 46 per cent remained habitable but required repairs. The flood also disrupted livelihoods, with over 158 farmlands submerged, posing a long-term threat to food security and income sources, particularly as in 72 per cent of the assessed location, scrop and vegetable farming remains the primary source of income for most residents in the affected areas. METHODOLOGY The Joint Flood Assessment by IOM’s DTM, NEMA, ADSEMA, NRCS, UNICEF, UNFPA, IRC, NRC, WHO and 20 other humanitarian partners in Yola South LGA employed direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions aimed at gathering data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrated field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for timely harmonised and reliable data collection. Data was triangulated across multiple sources for reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guided the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 15,128 Flood-affected population 202 House completely damaged 21 Functional health facilities after flooding 4,890 Displaced population 50 Water points completely damaged 865 T oilets/latrines affected 61 Water points partially damaged Figure 1. Key highlights 564 Houses flooded but in good condition 460 Houses partially damaged 7,148 Non-displaced population 158 Number of farmlands affected 290 Casualties (Injured 254| Lives lost 36) JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAMAWA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria The demographic analysis of the 15,128 individuals affected by flooding in Yola South LGA reveals a varied distribution across age and gender categories, underscoring the need for targeted, inclusive humanitarian responses. Adults aged 18–59 years constitute the largest segment of the affected population, making up 39 per cent in total (21% female, 18% male). Adolescents aged 13–17 years follow closely, representing 32 per cent of those affected, with females accounting for 17 per cent and males 15 per cent. Children between the ages of 1–5 years comprise 19 per cent of the population (10% female, 9% male), while infants under one year of age represent 6 per cent, evenly split at 3 per cent for both genders. The elderly population aged 60 years and above make up the smallest group at 4 per cent (2% female, 2% male). Overall, females represent a slightly higher proportion of the affected population at 53 per cent, compared to 47 per cent male. These demographic insights highlight the necessity for age and gender sensitive interventions, particularly in addressing the needs of adolescents, young children, and women of reproductive age. This was followed by Bako ward, which accounted for 2,829 individuals (449 households), making up about 19 per cent of the overall population. Makama ‘A’ ward reported 2,571 affected individuals (550 households), comprising 17 per cent of the total, while Makama ‘B’ ward had the lowest impact, with 1,020 individuals (170 households), representing 7 per cent of all those affected. JOINT FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — ADAWAMA STATE iomnigeriadtm@iom.int nigeria.iom.int dtm.iom.int/nigeria Following the flood incident that impacted over 15,128 individuals across the Bako, Bole Yolde Pate, Makama A, and Makama B wards of Yola South LGA, three priority needs were consistently identified by affected populations: shelter, food, and non-food items (NFIs), each representing a critical 100 per cent of the total assessed needs across all surveyed locations. Shelter was highlighted as the most immediate and urgent concern. Many households were rendered homeless or forced into makeshift and overcrowded spaces due to the complete or partial destruction of their homes. With 202 shelters destroyed and 1,226 others requiring repairs, affected families remain vulnerable to harsh weather conditions and health risks. Providing emergency shelter support is essential to protect lives, restore dignity, and reduce exposure to secondary risks such as disease outbreaks. Food insecurity has also become a major challenge in the aftermath of the flooding. With 158 farmlands submerged, access to regular food supplies has been severely disrupted. Families reported significant loss of food stocks, displacement from farmlands, and difficulty accessing local markets. Immediate food assistance is critical to prevent malnutrition, particularly among children, the elderly, and pregnant or lactating women. In addition, the need for NFIs including bedding, cooking utensils, hygiene kits, and clothing was reported across all assessed wards. Many households lost essential items due to the flood waters, further compounding daily struggles and deepening their vulnerability. Timely provision of NFIs will help restore basic living conditions and support the dignity and wellbeing of affected populations. The unanimous prioritization of shelter, food, and NFIs across all affected wards signals the need for a coordinated, multi-sectoral response. Addressing these urgent needs promptly will not only mitigate immediate suffering but also lay the groundwork for longer-term recovery and resilience in flood-affected communities. Many states have been impacted by this year's hefty rains, between August and September, resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. These floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have also exacerbated the situation, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. On 27 September 2025, the International Organization for Migration (IOM)’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in close coordination and collaboration with the Kogi State Emergency Management Agency (KOSEMA), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), the Kogi State Ministry of Health, the Kogi State Ministry of Transport, the State Coordinator National Hydroelectric Power Producing Areas Development Commission, Kogi State Fire Service, the National Inland Waterways Authority and the State Universal Basic Education Board, conducted a Joint Rapid Assessment (JRA) in response to flash flooding incident that affected a community in the wards of Oworo in Lokoja LGA. The assessment aimed to understand the extent of the flood’s impact on the affected population and infrastructure and to inform government and humanitarian partners on urgent needs, vulnerabilities, and displacement dynamics. The joint assessment identified 960 individuals (or 160 households) who were affected by the flood. Of these, 576 individuals (96 households) were displaced, while 384 individuals (64 households) remained within their communities as non-displaced. Approximately, 31 per cent of the affected houses were completely destroyed, 28 per cent were partially damaged, and 41 per cent remained habitable but required repairs. The flood also disrupted livelihoods, with farmland measuring up to 10 hectares submerged, posing a long-term threat to food security and income sources. METHODOLOGY The Joint Flood Assessment by IOM’s DTM, KOSEMA, NRCS and six other government agencies in Lokoja LGA employed direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions aimed at gathering data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrated field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for timely harmonized and reliable data collection. Data was triangulated across multiple sources while ethical principles and cultural awareness of local sensitivities guided the process. /reports/nigeria-joint-intention-survey-.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jul 21 2025 Jul 25 2025 Activity Survey Return Intention Benue State has experienced recurrent violence in recent years, particularly in rural areas where communities remain vulnerable to attacks and displacement. These incidents have disrupted lives and livelihoods, strained local coping mechanisms, and increased the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) across the state. On 13 and 14 June 2025, Yelwata community in Guma local government area (LGA) was attacked, resulting in loss of lives, destruction of property, and the displacement of thousands of residents. Survivors fled their homes, with many seeking refuge at the International Market IDPs Camp. While some arrived spontaneously, the government facilitated a formal relocation of affected persons. To support joint efforts toward durable solutions and safe, voluntary returns, IOM-DTM Nigeria, in collaboration with the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA) and key partners, conducted a Joint Intention Survey in the International Market IDPs Camp from 21 to 25 July 2025. This initiative was made possible through the combined efforts of the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA), the Benue State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the Benue State Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency (BERWASSA), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Catholic Caritas Foundation of Nigeria (CCFN), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) and the Jireh Doo Foundation (JDF). The collaboration underscores a unified commitment to building resilient communities and addressing the challenges faced by displaced populations. pdf_text.text: JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 Photo: Yelwata, Benue State © IOM 2025 / Elijah ELAIGWU 2,065 Interviewed HH 3 Average HH Size 38 Average Age of Respondents 14% Male Respondents 86% Female Respondents 9% Men 64% Children KEY FINDINGS 27% Women OVERVIEW Benue State has experienced recurrent violence in recent years, particularly in rural areas where communities remain vulnerable to attacks and displacement. These incidents have disrupted lives and livelihoods, strained local coping mechanisms, and increased the number of internally displaced persons (IDPs) across the state. On 13 and 14 June 2025, Yelwata community in Guma local government area (LGA) was attacked, resulting in loss of lives, destruction of property, and the displacement of thousands of residents. Survivors fled their homes, with many seeking refuge at the International Market IDPs Camp. While some arrived spontaneously, the government facilitated a formal relocation of affected persons. To support joint efforts toward durable solutions and safe, voluntary returns, IOM-DTM Nigeria, in collaboration with the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA) and key partners, conducted a Joint Intention Survey in the International Market IDPs Camp from 21 to 25 July 2025. This initiative was made possible through the combined efforts of the Benue State Emergency Management Agency (BSEMA), the Benue State Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the Benue State Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Agency (BERWASSA), the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), Catholic Caritas Foundation of Nigeria (CCFN), the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) and the Jireh Doo Foundation (JDF). The collaboration underscores a unified commitment to building resilient communities and addressing the challenges faced by displaced populations. The survey captures the return intentions and priorities of displaced households, providing insight into their current needs, challenges, and aspirations. These findings offer a basis for designing targeted interventions that are informed by the lived realities of the affected population and aimed at supporting their return and recovery. METHODOLOGY The primary objective of this survey was to understand the return intentions of households residing in the International Market IDPs Camp, specifically, their willingness and readiness to return to their place of origin, following the attack. A structured, face-to-face interview approach was adopted to allow for meaningful engagement and accommodate varying literacy levels among respondents. Enumerators visited each household in the camp and conducted interviews with the head of household. Where the head was unavailable, another senior household member was interviewed on their behalf. Responses were recorded digitally using tablets to ensure data accuracy and enable real-time entry and validation. Drawing on the population demography from the most recent joint registration exercise conducted at the camp, the baseline population stood at 2,336 households (5,294 individuals). A total of 2,065 households were successfully interviewed, representing a 99 per cent confidence level and a 1 per cent margin of error. This sample provides statistically significant and representative insights into the wider camp population. The survey tool was designed to collect information on household demographics, displacement history, and future intentions. It also explored factors influencing decisions to return or remain displaced, including safety, access to basic services, livelihoods, housing, and family ties. Ethical standards were upheld throughout the exercise. Participation was voluntary, informed consent was obtained from all respondents, and confidentiality was assured. Field supervisors conducted regular spot checks and reviewed submitted data daily to ensure quality control. Upon completion of data collection, responses were cleaned, analyzed, and shared with the Benue State Government and relevant partners to support policy formulation and programmatic planning. 1 JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 DISPLACEMENT HISTORY Findings from the Joint Intention Survey conducted at the International Market IDPs Camp showed that 90 per cent of households have experienced multiple displacements, while 10 per cent have been displaced only once. Among those displaced multiple times, 37 per cent have been displaced more than four times, 24 per cent four times, 20 per cent three times, and 9 per cent twice. This reflects the protracted and cyclical nature of displacement in Benue State, where recurrent violence continues to undermine community stability. Notably, 94 per cent of surveyed households reported that they were last displaced in 2025, a figure that aligns with the violent attack on Yelwata community in June 2025. This incident triggered a large-scale displacement of affected populations to the International Market IDPs Camp and underscores the urgent need for coordinated humanitarian assistance and the implementation of durable solutions to address both the immediate and long-term needs of affected households. INTENTION TO RETURN The survey on return intentions among camp residents offers valuable insights into the future aspirations of IDPs. Approximately 87 per cent of respondents expressed a strong desire to return to their place of origin, highlighting the enduring bond between displaced persons and their ancestral communities. This preference indicates that, despite the recent displacement and emerging challenges, most residents still consider their original homes as the most meaningful and ideal destination for resettlement. Conversely, 13 per cent of respondents indicated no intention to return. This group cited concerns such as insecurity, lack of basic services, and unresolved communal tensions as major deterrents. Their responses point to the need for targeted interventions that address these underlying challenges to ensure that any future return is both voluntary and sustainable. Among respondents who chose to return, 90 per cent indicated a preference to return with their entire household, highlighting the importance of family unity. Six per cent stated they would return alone, while four per cent noted they would not return with their family. 2 JOINT INTENTION SURVEY ─ BENUE STATE INTERNATIONAL MARKET IDPS CAMP ─ AUGUST 2025 10% 90% No Yes Fig 1: Multiple displacements 37% 24% 20% 10% 9% More than 4 times 4 times 3 times Once Twice Fig 2: Number of displacements 1% 2% 1% 1% <1% 94% Before 2016 2016 - 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Fig 3: Year of last displacement 13% 87% No Yes 90% 6% 4% We would return together I will return alone We would not return together Fig 4: Household return intention Fig 5: Planned phases of return REASONS FOR INTENDED RETURN Among respondents intending to return, the leading motivation was the search for livelihood opportunities, reported by 58 per cent of households. This reflects a strong desire for economic stability and self-reliance. Limited employment options at their current location served as a push factor for 45 per cent of respondents, reinforcing the urgency to seek better prospects. Additionally, family reunification was cited by 32 per cent, highlighting the emotional and social bonds that continue to influence return intentions, while 27 per cent expressed a desire to reclaim assets and properties. Other reasons included family ties (21%), improved security at the place of origin (20%), reconstruction needs (19%), and prospects for economic recovery (14%). REASONS FOR NOT RETURNING TO PLACE OF ORIGIN Among respondents who do not intend to return, several key conditions were identified that would need to be addressed before they could consider going back to their communities. The most cited reason was the absence of housing—either destroyed, damaged, or unavailable, reported by 77 per cent of households. Without a place to return to, many families remain unable to envision resettling in their area of origin. The fear of persecution or violence, was the second most prevalent barrier, mentioned by 65 per cent. Trauma and psychosocial distress from previous attacks, as well as the perception of ongoing threats, were highlighted by 58 per cent. Insecurity and the inaccessibility of return areas were cited by 48 per cent as critical concerns. Additionally, 23 per cent reported lacking the financial means to support their return journey, while 21 per cent noted that theft or loss of belongings during displacement presented a significant barrier to returning. HOUSING AVAILABLE/ACCESSIBLE AT INTENDED RETURN LOCATION Of the respondents who intend to return, 69 per cent reported having confirmation that housing was available or accessible at their place of origin. /reports/nigeria-joint-post-flood-situat.title: Nigeria — Joint Post - Flood Situation Report — 18 states (30 November 2024)
/reports/nigeria-joint-post-flood-situat.summary: Between 28 October and 8 November 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the respective State Emergency Management Agencies (SEMAs), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 1,078 locations in Adamawa, Anambra, Bayelsa, Cross River, Delta, Ebonyi, Edo, Enugu, Imo, Jigawa, Kebbi, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Niger, Oyo, Rivers and Taraba states that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessments were jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions.

NIGERIA (09 January 2025) JOINT POST–FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — KATSINA STATE OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and October. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 1 and 6 December 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Katsina State Emergency Management Agency (KATSEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 16 locations in Katsina State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced person (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of several key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessments was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the sixteen (16) local government areas (LGAs) of Katsina State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 119,309 individuals in 18,143 households that were affected by the floods. These individuals included both IDPs and residents who were impacted by the floods but remained in their affected communities. The affected population included 35,857 individuals and 16,431 returnees. T wenty-nine per cent (29%) of the affected houses were habitable but need repair, 23 per cent of the houses were partially damaged but need repairs and 27 per cent of the houses were completely destroyed. In 92 per cent (92%) of the locations assessed, crop farming was among the main sources of income.c METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 119,309 Flood-affected population 4,921 House completely damaged 10 No shelter 4,240 Houses partially damaged 61 Functional health facility after flooding 1,230 Casualties (Injured 1,138 | Lives lost 92) 35,857 Displaced population 39 Water points completely damaged 5,390 T oilets/latrines affected 54 Water points partially damaged 5 Main sources of livelihood 3,800 Number of farmlands affected Fig. 1. Children between 1 and 17 years represent a significant portion of the population, necessitating attention to their educational, nutritional, and protection needs. Adults (18-59 years), as the largest group, are expected to play a central role in recovery efforts and may need support to regain their livelihoods. The elderly, though a smaller group, remain particularly vulnerable and require special attention to health and mobility needs. The overall population consists of a higher percentage of females (62%) compared to males (38%), which must be taken into account in all aspects of the response. Gender-sensitive approaches should be incorporated into all aspects of the response. T emporary shelter solutions and long- term housing rehabilitation are essential to support affected communities and enable recovery. Food security was also a major concern, reported as the second most urgent need in 49 per cent of the locations assessed. This is likely attributed to disruptions in food supply chains, crop losses, and the destruction of livelihoods. Food was followed by non-food items (NFIs) in 34 per cent of the locations assessed: A significant portion of the population urgently requires essential items like blankets, clothing, cooking utensils, and hygiene products. This indicates widespread loss of personal belongings and limited access to basic necessities. The need for Psychosocial support was reported by 14 per cent of the assessed locations, underscoring significant mental health challenges in the aftermath of the disaster. Addressing these needs is vital for community recovery and resilience. Additionally, education services was highlighted in five per cent of the locations assessed, reflecting disruptions to schooling caused by the crisis. Health services, identified as a need in 13 per cent of the locations, require targeted interventions to address the immediate and long-term health impacts of the disaster. In conclusion, the most urgent needs identified include shelter, food, NFIs, psychosocial support, health, and education. In the eighteen (18) local government areas (LGAs) of Kebbi State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 280,230 individuals in 54,617 households affected by the floods. These individuals included 195,789 non-displaced individuals impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 66,532 displaced individuals. Twenty-five per cent (25%) of the affected houses were habitable but need repair, forty-five per cent of the houses were partially damaged and twenty-seven per cent were completely destroyed. In ninety-three per cent (93%) of the locations assessed, crop/vegetable farming was among the primary sources of income. Cite as

NIGERIA (09 January 2025) JOINT POST–FLOOD SITUATION REPORT — PLATEAU STATE OVERVIEW The rainy season in Nigeria typically occurs annually, with the highest concentration of rainfall between June and October. Many states have been impacted by hefty rains from July to October resulting in significant flooding that has devastated various communities. The floods have caused extensive damage to infrastructure, crops, and shelters, severely affecting livelihoods and displacing households. Climate variability and human-induced factors have exacerbated recently, leading to increased displacement across Nigeria. Between 1 and 6 December 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Plateau State Emergency Management Agency (PLSEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS), identified 19 locations in Plateau State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced person (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of several key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessments was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the nine (9) local government areas (LGAs) of Plateau State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 4,556 individuals in 906 households that were affected by the floods. These individuals included both IDPs and residents who were impacted by the floods but remained in their affected communities. The affected population included 83 individuals and 40 returnees. Three per cent (3%) of the affected houses were habitable but need repair, two per cent of the houses were partially damaged but need repairs and less than one per cent of the houses were completely destroyed. In 84 per cent (84%) of the locations assessed, crop farming was among the main sources of income.c METHODOLOGY The Joint Post-Flood Assessment employs direct observation, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions to gather data on the impact, living conditions and needs of flood-affected populations. Using a participatory approach, the assessment integrates field visits and remote interviews in inaccessible areas, leveraging collaboration with government and humanitarian partners for accurate data collection. Data is triangulated across multiple sources to ensure reliability, while ethical principles and cultural sensitivities guide the process. Findings provide actionable insights for government and humanitarian partners to address urgent needs and inform emergency response strategies. 4,556 Flood-affected population 8 House completely damaged 123 Houses partially damaged 61 Functional health facility after flooding 6 Casualties (Injured 5 | Lives lost 1) 83 Displaced population 13 Water points completely damaged 58 T oilets/latrines affected 16 Water points partially damaged 3 Main sources of livelihood 752 Number of farmlands affected Fig. 1. Children between 1 and 17 years represent a significant portion of the population, necessitating attention to their educational, nutritional, and protection needs. Adults (18-59 years), as the largest group, are expected to play a central role in recovery efforts and may need support to regain their livelihoods. The elderly, though a smaller group, remain particularly vulnerable and require special attention to health and mobility needs. The overall population consists of a higher percentage of females (55%) compared to males (45%), which must be taken into account in all aspects of the response. Gender-sensitive approaches should be incorporated into all aspects of the response. A significant portion of the population urgently requires essential items like blankets, clothing, cooking utensils, and hygiene products. This indicates widespread loss of personal belongings and limited access to basic necessities. Food security was also a major concern, reported as the second most urgent need in 89 per cent of the location assessed. This is likely attributed to disruptions in food supply chains, crop losses, and the destruction of livelihoods. Sixty-eight per cent of locations assessed need cash/vouchers , which could improve their livelihood by providing financial relief, enabling them to meet basic needs, and build resilience against unexpected events. Sixteen per cent of the locations need shelter assistance, reflecting damage to homes and displacement. T emporary shelter solutions, as well as long-term housing rehabilitation, will be essential to support the affected population. The equal demand for psychosocial support and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services highlights the significant and often overlooked mental health needs within affected communities alongside the critical need for restoring access to clean water and improving sanitation. This underscores the urgent need for integrated disaster response efforts that address both physical and mental health needs. Simultaneously, inadequate WASH services pose serious risks of disease outbreaks, further compromising the well-being of affected populations. Prioritizing both psychosocial support and WASH services is crucial for ensuring a comprehensive and effective response to the crisis. In conclusion, the most pressing needs are related to NFIs, food, cash/vouchers assistance, shelter, which require immediate attention. Efforts to address these areas will be critical in stabilizing the affected communities and helping them recover from the impacts of the floods. 100% of locations assessed 89% of locations assessed SHELTERFOOD Fig. 3. /reports/nigeria-joint-post-flood-situat.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact iomnigeriadtm@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Dec 01 2024 Dec 06 2024 Activity Mobility Tracking Event Tracking Between 1 and 6 December 2024, the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Yobe State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS) identified 99 locations in Yobe State that were impacted by floods or received internally displaced persons (IDPs) due to the flooding. Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessment was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the 17 local government areas (LGAs) of Yobe State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 88,901 individuals in 21,180 households affected by the floods. These individuals included 50,304 non-displaced individuals impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 20,212 displaced individuals. Thirty-one per cent (31%) of the affected houses were habitable but needed repair, twenty-five per cent of the houses were partially damaged and twenty per cent were completely destroyed. In all of the locations assessed, crop/vegetable farming was among the primary sources of income. Cite as

Through a network of key informants and field focal points, and in close coordination with other humanitarian partners and local authorities, the assessment was jointly conducted in these locations to provide insights to the government and humanitarian partners on the affected population's primary needs, vulnerabilities, and mobility intentions. In the twelve (12) local government areas (LGAs) of Zamfara State that were assessed, the joint assessment team identified 61,179 individuals in 10,179 households affected by the floods. These individuals included 39,440 non-displaced individuals impacted by the floods but remained in their communities. The affected population included 13,775 displaced individuals. Twenty-six per cent (26%) of the affected houses were habitable but needed repair, 19 per cent of the houses were partially damaged and 21 per cent were completely destroyed. In all of the locations assessed, crop/vegetable farming and petty trading were the primary sources of income. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-multi-sectoral-location.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jun 21 2021 Jul 30 2021 Activity Site Assessment Mobility Tracking Baseline Assessment This report presents a summary of the analysis of the Round 7 data collection of the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) Multi-Sectoral Location Assessment (MLSA) in the North Central and North West Geopolitical Zones of Nigeria and Round 38 of the DTM MSLA in the North East Geopolitical Zone. For the first time, these assessments specifically included energy-related questions. The assessment in the North Central and North West Regions was conducted through key informant interviews in a total of 1,604 locations across the Sates of Benue, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Nasarawa, Plateau, Sokoto, and Zamfara. The assessment was done between the 1st of July and the 29th of July 2021. In total, these locations host 833,006 Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) (134,908 households). The assessment in the North East Zone was conducted through key informant interviews in a total of 2,379 locations across the States of Adamawa, Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Taraba, and Yobe. The assessment was done between the 21st of June 2021 and the 30th of July 2021. In total, these locations host 2,182,613 IDPs (444,781 households). More information on the assessment methodology can be found in Section 5. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-national-displacement-p.summary: Following the release of the first edition of PROGRESS 2023 report , the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) has compiled a series of National Displacement Profiles based on end of year 2023 figures. These profiles offer insights into the latest end-of-year 2023 figures, aligning with the objectives outlined by the Data for Solutions to Internal Displacement Taskforce (DSID) .
/reports/nigeria-national-displacement-p.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Jan 01 2023 Dec 31 2023 Activity Survey Following the release of the first edition of PROGRESS 2023 report , the Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) has compiled a series of National Displacement Profiles based on end of year 2023 figures. These profiles offer insights into the latest end-of-year 2023 figures, aligning with the objectives outlined by the Data for Solutions to Internal Displacement Taskforce (DSID) . The profile provides a comprehensive overview of the demographic breakdowns and geographical distribution of internally displaced persons (IDPs) in Nigeria as of the end of 2023. It delves into the primary areas of origin and displacement for IDPs, shedding light on the factors influencing their decision-making processes regarding the selection of solutions locations. Additionally, the report discusses the obstacles encountered by IDPs in their pursuit of durable solutions. This compilation underscores the critical role of data in addressing internal displacement challenges and highlights the ongoing efforts to leverage data-driven solutions through collaborative initiatives like DSID. /reports/nigeria-nigeria-north-central-n.title: Nigeria — Nigeria — North Central & North West Flash Report 79 (29 November - 05 December 2021)
/reports/nigeria-nigeria-north-central-n.summary: Nigeria's North Central and North West Zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis that is rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). The crisis has accelerated during the past years because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region.
/reports/nigeria-nigeria-north-central-n.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact DTM Nigeria, AllUsersInDTMNigeria@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Nov 29 2021 Dec 05 2021 Activity Event Tracking Mobility Tracking Nigeria's North Central and North West Zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis that is rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). The crisis has accelerated during the past years because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. In the evening of 3 December 2021, Sabon Birni town in Sabon Birni LGA in the state of Sokoto was attacked by armed bandits. Following this event, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff with the purpose of informing the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations. Cite as

/reports/nigeria-nigeria-north-central-n.title: Nigeria — Nigeria — North Central & North West Flash Report 87 (24 - 30 January 2022)
/reports/nigeria-nigeria-north-central-n.summary: Nigeria's north-central and north-west zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). During the past years, the crisis has accelerated because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. Between the 24th and 30th of January 2022, armed clashes between herders and farmers; and bandits and local communities have led to new waves of population displacement. Following these events, rapid assessments were conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff to inform the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-and-north.summary: Round 12 of DTM data collection in Nigeria’s north-west and north-central regions was conducted between 13 September and 24 October 2023. During the activity, DTM deployed teams of enumerators to conduct assessments in 826 wards (down from the 881 wards assessed in Round 11 of DTM assessments), located in 172 LGAs (down from 180 LGAs in Round 11). Eight states were covered: Benue, Nasarawa and Plateau (north-central) and Kaduna, Kano, Sokoto, Katsina and Zamfara (north-west). DTM enumerators conducted assessments in 1,637 locations (a decrease of 121 locations compared to Round 11), including 1,549 (95%) locations where IDPs were residing among host communities and 88 (5%) locations categorized as camps/camp-like settings. The reason for the decrease owed to the inaccessibility of some locations caused by security. During these assessments, data was collected on population demographics, living conditions and multisectoral needs of displaced populations.

It examines the spatial distribution of internally displaced persons (IDPs) and returnees, alongside key drivers of displacement, duration of displacement, and the living conditions and intentions of affected populations. The assessment was conducted by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in collaboration with the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), State Emergency Management Agencies (SEMAs), and the Nigerian Red Cross Society (NRCS). It covered 10 states—Benue, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kogi, Nasarawa, Niger, Plateau, Sokoto, and Zamfara, spanning 2,427 locations across 1,003 wards and 208 local government areas (LGAs). Data collection was undertaken between January and February 2026 through key informant interviews with community leaders, government officials, humanitarian partners, and displaced populations residing in both host communities and camp-like settings. As of February 2026, a total of 1,311,026 IDPs in 233,258 households were identified, reflecting an approximate 5 per cent decline compared to Round 18. MOBILITY TRACKING - IDP ATLAS NIGERIA - NORTH-CENTRAL AND NORTH-WEST ROUND 16 (FEBRUARY 2025) EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The report, presents the results from Round 16 of Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessments carried out by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which aims to improve and better understand the dynamics and trend of the internal displacement in the north-central and north-west conflict-affected region. This atlas was assessed between October and November 2024 and reflects the number of IDPs from the ten states in Nigeria’s north-central and north-west geopolitical zone. The zone is the most affected by th e conflict after the north-east and consists of Benue, Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Kogi, Niger, Nasarawa, Plateau, Sokoto and Zamfara states. In Round 16, 1,322,766 internally displaced persons (IDPs) were identified in 225,458 households. This represents a slight increase of approximately 10 per cent (or 130,350 individuals) compared to Round 15. One of the major reasons for such increase is due to the addition of new locations assessed. More so, other reasons could be attributed to attacks and displacements, disasters, seasonal mobility due to farming or in search of safety, security, or better services, etc. During Round 16, IDP assessment was conducted in 1,761 locations across the 10 north-central and north-west Nigeria states. The assessed locations included 104 camps and camp-like settlements and 1,657 locations where IDPs lived among host communities, recorded in November 2024. METHODOLOGY The IDP atlas is the product of the DTM Master list assessment which gathers data at site/location level using multiple key informants and direct observations. Interviews were conducted face-to-face by DTM in accessible locations. The atlas provides data on the number of IDPs at the state, local government area, ward and location levels, their shelter type, the period of displacement, and the areas of origin. The Master list presents data on the number of individuals and households using either head count, previous registration, official documentation or a demographic calculator based on a sample of assessed IDPs dispersed in host communities, camps or camp-like settings. LIMITATIONS • Insecurity remains the major hindrance to DTM assessments in the North-central and North-west, limitiing the field teams’ access to some locations with returnees and IDPs. • Transportation of many remote and hard-to-reach areas have become more difficult due to inflation in the cost of transportation. • Some enumerators experienced hesitance and reluctance from IDPs to cooperate with the surveys as data is collected regularly and assistance is limited. • The data used for this analysis were estimates obtained through key informant interviews, direct observation and focus group discussions. Thus, to ensure these estimates’ reliability, data collection was performed at the lowest administrative level: the site or the host community. POPULATION CATEGORY The population category defined in this report is as follows: • An Internally Displaced Person (IDP) according to DTM definition is ‘a person who has been forced to flee or to leave his or her home or place of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who has not crossed an internationally recognized state border.’ MOBILITY TRACKING - IDP ATLAS NIGERIA - NORTH-CENTRAL AND NORTH-WEST ROUND 16 (FEBRUARY 2025) ESTIMATED NUMBER OF IDPs The IOM’s supports the Government and humanitarian partners by establishing a comprehensive system that collects, analyses and disseminates data on IDPs to ensure timely and effective assistance to the affected populations. Data collection occurs at a granular level and is repeated regularly to ensure accurate and up-to-date information. As of November 2024, DTM identified a total of 1,322,766 IDPs in 225,458 households across Benue, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kogi, Nasarawa, Niger, Plateau, Sokoto, and Zamfara states. The data collection started in October 2024 in 1,761 locations, in the 10 states of north-central and north-west Nigeria. The IDP population included IDPs in camps and camp-like settings (239,862 individuals or 18%) and host communities (1,082,904 individuals or 82%). This signifies an IDP increase of approximately 10 per cent or 130,350 IDPs compared to what it was in June 2024. One of the major reason for such increase is due to the addition of new locations assessed. Matrix (DTM) assessments carried out by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), which aims to improve and better understand the dynamics and trend of the internal displacement in the north-central and north-west conflict-affected region. This atlas was assessed between September and October 2025 and reflects the number of IDPs and returnees from 10 states in Nigeria’s north-central and north-west geopolitical zone. In both regions, the most affected zones are Benue, Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Kogi, Niger, Nasarawa, Plateau, Sokoto and Zamfara states. As of October 2025, the region hosts 1,378,124 internally displaced persons (IDPs) and 428,969 returnees. IDPs are predominantly found in host communities (81%), with smaller proportions in camps, integrated settings, or relocated sites. The primary causes are armed banditry/kidnapping (54%), farmer-herder clashes (33%), communal clashes (7%), climate-related disasters (3%), and insurgency (2%). These factors vary by state and period, with armed banditry/kidnapping remaining the dominant trigger. Benue State leads in both IDP (464,543; 34%) and returnee (143,887; 34%) populations. Kogi State is the second largest for returnees (108,443; 25%), while Katsina and Kaduna also report significant figures. At the LGA level, Ibaji (Kogi) and several LGAs in Benue are major returnee hotspots. While progress is evident in the scale of returns in certain states and LGAs, significant challenges remain. Many areas continue to experience new displacement, and conditions for sustainable return are not uniformly present. The Atlas serves as a critical tool for planning, resource allocation, and advocacy, supporting efforts to restore safety, dignity, and opportunity for displaced and returning populations in the regions. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The IDP and returnee atlas is the product of the DTM Master list assessment which gathers data at site/location level using multiple key informants and direct observations. Interviews are conducted face-to- face by DTM in accessible locations. The atlas provides data on the number of IDPs and returnees at the state, local government area, ward and location levels, their shelter type, the period of displacement, the areas of origin for IDPs and the areas of last displacement for returnees. The Master list presents data on the number of individuals and households using head count, previous registration, official documentation or a demographic calculator based on a sample of assessed IDPs dispersed in host communities, camps or camp-like settings. METHODOLOGY POPULATION CATEGORY The population categories are defined in this report as follows: • An internally displaced person (IDP) according to DTM definition is a person who has been forced to flee or to leave his or her home or place of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights or natural or human-made disasters, and who has not crossed an internationally recognized state border. • IDPs on a pathway to a durable solution are displaced persons who, while still displaced, is progressively addressing their displacement-related needs, such as safety, housing, livelihoods, access to services, and rights, so they can sustainably rebuild their lives through local integration, return, or relocation elsewhere in the country. Integrated IDPs are displaced persons who have assimilated into the local community, in the location that they were displaced to. Relocated IDPs are displaced persons who have physically moved (voluntarily or through organized relocation programs) from camps, unsafe areas, or high-risk zones to a new settlement/site. • In the context of Nigeria, a returnee is defined by DTM as any former IDP who returned to his or her locality of origin (IDP returnee); or any former refugee who returned to his or her country of origin (returnee from abroad). Return is understood as a physical return and does not imply or suggest that returnees live in a safe environment with dignity and access to sustainable livelihood opportunities or adequate resources. LIMITATIONS • In some north-central and north-west Nigeria LGAs, the security situation remains volatile. Therefore, not all locations were accessible at the time of the assessment. In Zamfara state, some locations in Maru, Shinkafi and Zurmi LGAs were not accessible during this round. •

pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 5 and 10 May 2025, multiple farmer-herder clashes occurred across 10 communities in the local government areas (LGA) of Makurdi, Ukum, Otukpo, Apa, Logo, and Guma in Benue State. These clashes affected 634 individuals across 117 households and resulted in 80 casualties, including 50 injuries and 30 fatalities. The affected communities include Akpete in Ojantelle ward of Apa LGA; Tse-Umande in Mbabai ward of Guma LGA; Ayilamo and Tse Nyamkyume in Tombo ward of Logo LGA; Nyijir, Tse Amela, and Tse Hungu in Mbalagh ward of Makurdi LGA; Otobi-Ankpa in Otobi ward of Otukpo LGA; Jootar in Mbayenge ward; and Zaki Biam in Uyam ward of Ukum LGA. The incidents displaced 271 individuals, with 258 moving from Tse-Umande to Daudu Camp 2 in Mbawa ward and 13 from Tse Nyamkyume to Ayilamo community, while the remaining affected individuals stayed in their communities. Among the affected individuals were 272 children, 208 women, and 154 men. Of all the needs identified, non-food items (NFI), food, WASH and security were the most prevalent. Other needs included health and psychosocial support. Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria's north-central region has been experiencing a prolonged crisis. Historical tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, often lead to conflicts, attacks, and banditry or hirabah. These incidents may involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. In recent years, the crisis has intensified, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-central regions. pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 16 and 18 May 2025, multiple incidents of farmer-herder clashes and non-state armed group attacks occurred across five communities in the local government areas (LGAs) of Agatu, Guma, Logo and Ukum in Benue State. These incidents affected 232 individuals across 40 households, displaced 64 individuals and resulted in 11 casualties, including three injuries and eight fatalities. The affected communities include Tse Bamun in Kundav ward and Afia in Tsaav ward of Ukum LGA; Tsukwa in Mbagber ward of Logo LGA; Ogumogbo in Usha ward of Agatu LGA; and Tse-Orkpen in Mbabai ward of Guma LGA. The incidents displaced 26 individuals from Tse-Orkpen in Mbabai ward to Daudu in Mbawa ward of Guma LGA and 38 individuals from Ogumogbo to a neighbouring community of Oweto in Usha ward, while 168 affected individuals remained in their communities. Among the affected individuals were 127 children, 60 women, and 45 men. Of all the needs identified, security, non-food items (NFI), health and food were the most prevalent. Other needs included shelter, WASH and psychosocial support. Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria's north-central region has been experiencing a prolonged crisis. Historical tensions between farmers and herders, as well as ethnic and religious groups, often lead to conflicts, attacks, and banditry or hirabah. These incidents may involve kidnapping and theft along major highways. In recent years, the crisis has intensified, resulting in widespread displacement across the north-central regions. /reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Between 27 and 31 August 2024, armed bandits attacked the communities of Naka Agagbe Road in Mbachohon ward and Tse Ugbadu in Sagher Ukusu ward of Gwer West local government area (LGA), Tinenune and Dyom HC in Mbatian ward and Tse Aye in Kendev ward of Ukum LGA  and farmer/herders clashes occured in the community of Ugbe in Moon ward of Kwande LGA, all in Benue State. There were reports of 107 injuries and 15 fatalities. The attacks affected 497 individuals in 94 households and the farmer/herders clashes affected four individuals in four households. The affected individuals included 199 children, 145 women and 158 men. On 26 August 2024, armed bandits attacked the community of Kurmin B in Angunu ward of Kachia LGA in Kaduna State. There were reports of six injuries and two fatalities. The attack affected 95 individuals in 18 households. The affected individuals included 64 children, 18 women and 13 men. Also, on 29 August 2024, armed bandits attacked the community of Katsalle in Yan-tumaki A ward of Dan Musa LGA in Katsina State. The attack affected 993 individuals in 132 households. The affected individuals included 694 children, 191 women and 108 men.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.title: Nigeria — North-central & North-west Flash Report #100 (2 - 8 May 2022)
/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Nigeria's north-central and north-west zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). During the past years, the crisis has accelerated because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. Between the 2nd and 8th of May 2022, armed clashes and banditry have led to new waves of population displacement. Following these events, rapid assessments were conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff to inform the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations. During the assessment period, the DTM identified an estimated 1,973 individuals who were affected by the attacks. A total of 1,912 individuals were displaced to neighbouring wards in the LGAs Bakura, Maradun and Tsafe in Zamfara State and Jibia in Katsina State. A total of 131 casualties were reported, including 70 injuries and 61 fatalities.

Following these events, a rapid assessment was conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staﬀ to inform the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of aﬀected populations. During the assessment period, the DTM identified an estimated 3,460 individuals who were aﬀected by the attacks and 318 individuals by the rainstorms. A total of 3,458 individuals were displaced to neighbouring wards in Kankara and Batsari LGAs of Katsina state as a result of the attacks and rainstorms displaced 96 individuals in Ingawa LGA of Katsina state and 222 individuals in Doguwa LGA of Kano state from their places of residence to neighbouring communities. A total of 32 casualties were reported, including 30 injuries and 2 fatalities. Cite as

The fire outbreak affected 28 individuals, who are currently in neighbouring shelters. The fire outbreak damaged a total of 9 shelters, of which 3 shelters are completely damaged and 6 shelter are partially damaged.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.title: Nigeria — North-central & North-west Flash Report 160 (18 - 24 March 2024)
/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Armed bandits launched a series of attacks in the states of Zamfara and Kaduna between 18 and 24 March 2024. Maradaw, Gusami, Maikuru, and Masha Awo settlements in Gusami Ward of Birnin Magaji LGA were affected in Zamfara State. The affected settlements in Kaduna State were Ungwan Mai Ido Rafi in Ankwa Ward (in Kachia LGA), Dogon Noma in Maro Ward, and Kajuru Station in Tantatu Ward, (all in Kajuru LGA). The attacks destroyed the possessions of many local households and also destroyed 58 shelters. Two fatalities and thirty-one injuries were reported. A total of 361 households and 2,162 individuals were affected by the attacks. There were 934 children, 714 women, and 514 males among the affected persons. A total of 1,943 individuals were displaced as a result of the attacks. A total of 680 individuals were displaced from Gusami Gari Ward in Birnin Magaji LGA to Chakal community in Tudun Wada of Gusau LGA in Zamfara State. Furthermore, a total of 1,032 individuals were displaced from Ungwan Mai Ido Rafi community in Ankwa Ward to Kachia Urban in Kachia Ward all in Kachia LGA of Kaduna State. A total of 231 individuals were displaced from Tantatu Ward to Maraba Kajuru in Kufana Ward all in Kajuru LGA. Meanwhile, there was no displacement out of Dogon Noma community as affected individuals remained in the location. Of all the needs identified, food and shelter were the most prevalent. Other needs include non-food items (NFI), security and psychosocial support.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.title: Nigeria — North-central & North-west Flash Report 161 (25 - 31 March 2024)
/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: On 27 March 2024, armed bandits attacked the community of Mutunji in Maru ward of Maru LGA in Zamfara State. There were no reports of injuries and fatalities. The attack displaced 230 individuals in 42 households to Tsunami community in Rijya ward of Gusau LGA of Zamfara State. The displaced individuals included 129 children and 101 women. The men in the community decided to stay back. Of all the needs identified, food and shelter were the most prevalent. Other needs included security and non-food items (NFI). Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria’s North-central and North-west zones are afflicted with a multi-dimensional crisis. Long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups often result in attacks and banditry or hirabah. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. During the past years, the crisis accelerated and has resulted in widespread displacement across the North-central and North-west regions.

On 30 November 2024, armed bandits attacked the communities of Anguwa Magiro in Bass/Kukoki ward, Shiroro LGA of Niger State. This attack affected a total of 285 individuals in 30 households, including 219 children, 39 women and 27 men.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Between 12 and 13 December 2024, armed bandits attacked the communities of Kuringafa in Tsauri ‘A’ ward of Kurfi local government area (LGA) and Dankumeji in Mabai ward, Kankara LGA, all in Katsina State. This attack affected 879 individuals across 103 households, including 527 children, 189 women, and 163 men, resulting in 16 injuries and 16 fatalities.
/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.body: Share View all bookmarks Download Share Contact iomnigeriadtm@iom.int Language English Location Nigeria Period Covered Dec 12 2024 Dec 13 2024 Activity Mobility Tracking Event Tracking Between 12 and 13 December 2024, armed bandits attacked the communities of Kuringafa in Tsauri ‘A’ ward of Kurfi local government area (LGA) and Dankumeji in Mabai ward, Kankara LGA, all in Katsina State. This attack affected 879 individuals across 103 households, including 527 children, 189 women, and 163 men, resulting in 16 injuries and 16 fatalities. Of all the needs identified, health and security were the most prevalent. Other needs included non-food items (NFI), food, and psychosocial support. Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria’s north-central and north-west zones are afflicted with a multi-dimensional crisis. Long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups often result in attacks and banditry or hirabah. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. During the past years, the crisis accelerated and has resulted in widespread displacement across the north-central and north-west regions. Cite as

On 05 January 2025, armed bandits attacked the community of Tse Abari Shor in Ugbaam ward of Ukum LGA in Benue State. The attack affected 37 individuals across eight households, including 18 children, 12 women, and seven men, resulting in one injury.

/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Between 31 March and 03 April 2025, natural disasters and multiple incidents of violence affected communities in 10 locations across Benue and Zamfara States, in North-west and North-central Nigeria, resulting in 3,180 displaced individuals, 210 damaged shelters and 53 casualties.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 31 March and 03 April 2025, multiple incidents of violence and natural disasters affected several communities across Benue and Zamfara States, displacing 3,180 Individuals. Between 31 March and 03 April 2025, armed bandits attacked the communities of Asa in Otukpo Town West Ward and Bornbricks in Otobi Ward (both in Otukpo LGA), Anmoda in Oglewu Ward (Ohimini LGA), and Achagh in Tijime Ward (Gwer West LGA) in Benue State. These attacks impacted 95 individuals from 22 households, including 45 children, 23 women, and 27 men, resulting in nine injuries and six fatalities. On 02 April 2025 in Benue State, a communal clash erupted between the communities of Paun and Abayol in Mbagwe Ward, Ushongo LGA, displacing 81 individuals from 16 households to the Mbaise community within the same ward. Among those affected were 31 children, 28 women, and 22 men, with two individuals injured. Additionally, on 02 and 03 April 2025, farmer-herder clashes were reported in the communities of Mbavyuur Mbahini (Gbemacha Ward, Gwer East LGA), Abua (Fildi Ward, Makurdi LGA), and Tse Gyenku (Ugbaam Ward, Ukum LGA), affecting 245 individuals across 44 households. These incidents impacted 112 children, 80 women, and 53 men, resulting in four injuries and one fatality. Also, on 02 April 2025, rainfall combined with ongoing construction of a water channel along Vandikiya Street in Wailomayo Ward (Makurdi LGA) caused flooding, impacting 83 individuals from 19 households. The affected population included 33 children, 27 women, and 23 men. On 03 April 2025, armed bandits attacked Rijiya community in Rijiya Ward, Gusau LGA, Zamfara State. The attack affected 2,676 individuals across 496 households, with 30 individuals from 12 households displaced to Garage Mai Lena community. The casualties included 1,499 children, 643 women, and 534 men, resulting in 10 injuries and 21 fatalities. Of all the needs identified, security, non-food items (NFI), food, health and psychosocial support were the most prevalent. Other needs included shelter, WASH and transport. Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria’s north-central and north-west zones are afflicted with a multi-dimensional crisis. Long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups often result in attacks and banditry or hirabah. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. During the past years, the crisis accelerated and has resulted in widespread displacement across the north-central and north-west regions. Individuals Aﬀected 3,180 *Multiple choices selected Fig. 1. The clashes affected 1,391 individuals across 315 households and displaced 171 individuals from Otobi-Ankpa in Otobi ward of Otukpo LGA to Mbasombo ward of Gwer East LGA and 96 individuals from Emichi to neighbouring ward of Otukpo Town Central. The affected individuals included 592 children, 453 women, and 346 men, resulting in 156 injuries and 55 fatalities. Also, on 16 and 17 April 2025, a heavy rainfall occurred in Makurdi LGA affecting Mega camp, Abagena camp, Ichwa camp in Agan ward and Adaka camp in Modern Market ward. All in Benue State. The rainfall affected 238 individuals across 57 households. The affected individuals included 76 children, 101 women, and 61 men. On 17 April 2025, armed bandits attacked the community of Tashar Biri in Yantumaki B ward of Dan Musa LGA in Katsina State. The attack affected 208 individuals across 29 households. The affected individuals included 116 children, 50 women and 42 men, resulting in three injuries and five fatalities. In addition, on 14 and 19 April 2025, armed bandits attacked the communities of Zikke/Kwall in Kimikpa ward of Bassa LGA and Darin, Daku, Tan-jol and Vwak in Jol/Kwi ward of Riyom LGA, all in Plateau State. The attack affected 1,014 individuals across 207 households and 331 individuals from the community Zikke/Kwall to Jebbu Miango and Miango in Taagbe ward of Bassa LGA and 552 individuals from the communities of Darin, Daku, Tan-jol and Vwak to Riyom community hall in Riyom ward. The affected individuals included 568 children, 291 women, and 155 men, resulting in 26 injuries and 53 fatalities. The attack affected 6,688 individuals across 1,347 households and displaced 151 individuals to the neighbouring communities. The affected individuals included 3,744 children, 1,628 women and 1,316 men, resulting in 28 injuries and 40 fatalities. Of all the needs identified, shelter, non-food items (NFI) and food were the most prevalent. Other needs included security, health, WASH, transport and psychosocial support. These clashes affected 1,107 individuals across 234 households and displaced 63 individuals from Tse-Beeku to Daudu in Mbawa Ward, 197 individuals from Tse-Igbo to Ortese Camp in Nyiev Ward of Guma LGA, 318 individuals from Agbo Vengav to Aondoana in Tijime Ward of Gwer West, 67 individuals from Ikyurav-ya to Ikyogen in Liev II Ward of Kwande LGA, and 128 individuals from Antsah to Anini in North Bank I Ward of Makurdi LGA. The affected individuals included 505 children, 374 women, and 228 men, resulting in 89 injuries and 34 fatalities. On 22 April 2025, heavy rainfall occurred, affecting Idye community in Wailomayo Ward of Makurdi LGA in Benue State. The rainfall affected 206 individuals across 49 households. Among those affected were 56 children, 78 women, and 72 men. On 24 April 2025, armed bandits attacked the community of Njor in Avihijime Ward of Gwer West LGA in Benue State and kidnapped 30 individuals. The affected individuals included one child, 12 women, and 17 men, resulting in two injuries. On 27 April 2025, unknown gunmen attacked the community of Akpehe in Wailomayo Ward of Makurdi LGA in Benue State. The attack affected 46 individuals across 10 households. The affected individuals included 16 children, 12 women, and 18 men, resulting in three injuries and seven fatalities. /reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Between 28 April and 4 May 2025, multiple incidents of violence, including farmer-herder clashes, and armed bandit attacks occurred in 11 communities across Benue, Sokoto, and Zamfara states, affecting 7,668 individuals.

pdf_text.text: Event Overview Between 28 April and 4 May 2025, multiple incidents of violence, including farmer-herder clashes, and armed bandit attacks occurred in 11 communities across Benue, Sokoto, and Zamfara states, affecting 7,668 individuals. Between 28 April and 4 May 2025, farmer-herder clashes occurred in the communities of Ngban in Nyiev ward of Guma local government area (LGA), Ayar in Mbalom ward of Gwer east LGA, Tse Anungwa in Kundav ward of Ukum LGA, Akpete in Akpete/Ojantelle ward and Okwiji in Edikwu I ward of Apa LGA, all in Benue State. These clashes affected 341 individuals across 88 households and displaced 115 individuals from Ngban to Ortese camp in Nyiev, 81 individuals from Ayar to Ikpayango in Mbasombo ward, and 24 individuals from Akpete to Ugbokpo in Ugbokpo ward of Apa LGA. The affected individuals included 149 children, 111 women, and 81 men, resulting in 13 injuries and 14 fatalities. Also, between 28 April and 4 May 2025, armed bandits attacked the communities of Ugondo in Ikyaghev ward and Tyolaha in Sagher/Ukusu ward in Gwer West LGA, and Adoka in Adoka Icho ward of Otukpo LGA, all in Benue State. The attack affected 213 individuals across 25 households. The affected individuals included 115 children, 53 women, and 45 men, resulting in six injuries and five fatalities. On 4 May 2025, armed bandits attacked the communities of Satiru, Makwaruwa and Gidan Gyara in Bargaja ward of Isa LGA and Kubutta in Tursa ward of Rabah LGA, all in Sokoto State. The attack affected 6,795 individuals across 1,416 households and displaced 4,861 individuals from Satiru, Makwaruwa and Gidan Gyara to Isa, Sabon Birni, Lajinge and Unguwar Lalle in Unguwar Lalle ward in Sabon Birni LGA and 1,934 individuals from Kubutta to Achida, Wurno and Sokoto in Achida ward of Wurno LGA. The affected individuals included 3,806 children, 1,952 women, and 1,037 men, resulting in 74 injuries and 10 fatalities. Also, on 4 May 2025, armed bandits attacked the community of Nasarawa in Bakura ward of Bakura LGA in Zamfara State. The attack affected 319 individuals across 70 households and displaced 26 individuals from Nasarawa to Lambar Bakura Durawu in Danmanau ward of Bakura LGA. The affected individuals included 181 children, 76 women, and 62 men, resulting in four injuries. Of all the needs identified, food, non-food items (NFI), shelter and security were the most prevalent. Other needs included WASH, health and psychosocial support. Following these events, DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff conducted rapid assessments to inform the humanitarian community and Government/partners, and to enable a targeted response. Nigeria’s north-central and north-west zones are afflicted with a multi-dimensional crisis. Long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups often result in attacks and banditry or hirabah. These attacks involve kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways by criminal groups. During the past years, the crisis accelerated and has resulted in widespread displacement across the north-central and north-west regions. Individuals Aﬀected 7,668 *Multiple choices selected Fig. 2. /reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.title: Nigeria — North Central & North West Flash Report #71 (04 – 10 October 2021)
/reports/nigeria-north-central-north-wes.summary: Nigeria's North Central and North West Zones are afflicted with a multidimensional crisis that is rooted in long-standing tensions between ethnic and religious groups and involves attacks by criminal groups and banditry/hirabah (such as kidnapping and grand larceny along major highways). The crisis has accelerated during the past years because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. Between 04 and 10 October 2021, armed clashes between herdsmen and farmers; and bandits and local communities have led to new waves of population displacement. Following these events, rapid assessments were conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff with the purpose of informing the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations. During the assessment period, the DTM identified an estimated number of 2,866 individuals who were displaced to neigbouring wards. A total of 55 injuries and 59 casualties were reported in the LGAs Batsari in Katsina State, Isa in Sokoto, Maradun in Zamfara State and Guma in Benue State.

During the past years, the crisis has accelerated because of the intensification of attacks and has resulted in widespread displacement across the region. Between the 7th and 13th of February 2022, armed clashes between herders and farmers; and bandits and local communities have led to new waves of population displacement. Following these events, rapid assessments were conducted by DTM (Displacement Tracking Matrix) field staff to inform the humanitarian community and government partners, and enable targeted response. Flash reports utilise direct observation and a broad network of key informants to gather representative data and collect information on the number, profile and immediate needs of affected populations. During the assessment period, the DTM identified an estimated 1,427 individuals who were affected by the attacks. A total of 1,406 individuals were displaced to neighbouring wards in the LGAs Bakori in Katsina State and Zangon Kataf in Kaduna State. A total of 33 casualties were reported, including 12 injuries and 21 fatalities. Cite as
